opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot. A few directions seem most promising to me.

The first is understanding what these models can and can't represent. With state space models, and recurrent models generally, you compress the entire history into a fixed-size state. That's the source of their efficiency, but it's also a real constraint. A lot of recent theoretical work tries to pin this down: which tasks need a state that grows with the sequence, like exact copying or associative recall over long contexts, and which can be solved with a compressed state? I think we'll get a much sharper picture of that trade-off, and ideally that will turn into practical guidance about when to use which kind of layer, instead of a fuzzy sense that attention is better at recall.

The second is the connection between different model families. One thing that's been exciting to me is that once you look closely, state space models, linear attention, and certain gated recurrences turn out to be closely related. They're all ways of parameterizing structured matrices that mix information along the sequence. That framing opened up a lot. It lets you move algorithms and hardware tricks from one family to another, and it makes the design space look more unified. I think the theory will keep pushing in that direction, toward a more general understanding of sequence mixing that treats attention and SSMs as points in a larger space rather than rivals.

Third, and this is the one I find most interesting conceptually, is understanding these models as compressors, and thinking about what makes a good state. Intuitively, a recurrent model has to decide online what to remember and what to forget. Selectivity in Mamba was one step toward making that decision data-dependent. But we don't yet have a very principled theory of what an ideal state looks like for, say, language versus audio versus DNA. There's probably a link to ideas from online learning and memory, like viewing the state update as a kind of optimization step, and some recent work has explored that. I'd like to see that become more rigorous.

And finally, hybrids. Empirically, mixing a few attention layers with mostly SSM layers works really well, but our understanding of why, and what the right ratio or placement is, is still mostly empirical. A theory explaining how the two kinds of layers divide the work would be really valuable.

So overall, I think the field is moving from "here's a new architecture that's fast" toward "here's a principled account of the trade-offs between memory, compute, and expressivity." That's where I hope the theory goes.

r001.rationale: It connects state space models, linear attention, and gated recurrences as ways to parameterize structured matrices that mix information along sequences, explicitly describing a shared structured-matrix view.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot. I'd say the thing I'm most excited about is that we're finally starting to get a real theory of what these models are actually doing, as opposed to just "here's a thing that works empirically." For a long time the story around state space models was mostly architectural: we figured out that if you parameterize the state update a certain way, you get something efficient to train and fast at inference. But the deeper question is what kind of computation that update is performing, and why selectivity matters so much.

One direction I think is really promising is the connection to associative memory and in-context learning. If you look at the recurrence in Mamba-2 or in linear attention variants, you can reinterpret the state as a kind of fast-weight memory that's being written to and read from, and the selection mechanism is basically a learned rule for when to write and when to forget. Once you frame it that way, you can start asking much sharper questions. What's the capacity of that memory? What kinds of retrieval are easy and which are fundamentally hard? Why do these models struggle with certain copying or lookup tasks, and what would it take to fix that in a principled way rather than by just bolting on attention layers?

The second direction is the duality stuff, the state space duality framing, where you show that a bunch of recurrent models and a bunch of attention variants are really the same object viewed through different lenses, structured matrices in particular. I think that's going to keep paying off. It gives you a unified language, so instead of "transformers versus SSMs" as a tribal thing, you get a design space where you can ask what structure you want in the mixing matrix and what that buys you in expressivity and compute.

And then the third thing, which is maybe more speculative, is understanding what the right notion of "state" even is. Tokens are a very arbitrary way to chop up data. I have a suspicion that a lot of the inefficiencies we see are artifacts of tokenization, and that models with a compressed state might actually be better suited to learning their own units, to operating on raw bytes or raw signals and discovering the structure themselves. If the theory can tell us what a good state representation looks like, that's where I think the next real jump comes from, not from squeezing a few more points out of the same setup.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the interesting directions is understanding what the state actually needs to remember. In a state space model, you’re compressing the history into a fixed-size state, so there’s a fundamental question about what information you can preserve and what kinds of tasks that representation supports.

With Mamba, the update depends on the input, which lets the model be selective about what it retains. But that also makes the analysis more challenging. We’d like to understand when that selectivity is enough, where the limitations are, and how those limitations change as you increase the state size.

The hope is that theory can guide architecture design. If we understand why a model struggles with a particular kind of retrieval or long-range dependency, that might tell us whether we need a different state update, more memory, or a combination with attention. I think that connection between understanding the mechanism and making practical design decisions is especially promising.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the interesting questions is understanding what the selection mechanism really buys you. With a structured state space model, you have this connection to linear systems, which gives you a fairly clean mathematical framework. But once the dynamics depend on the input, the model becomes much more expressive, and some of those tools no longer apply directly.

So I’d like to understand which kinds of sequence problems actually require that input dependence. When does selectively remembering or forgetting information make a fundamental difference? And how does that compare with having access to the entire history through attention?

There’s also a gap between showing that a model can represent some computation and explaining whether it can learn that computation efficiently. I think connecting expressivity, optimization, and memory requirements would be especially useful. Ideally, the theory would help us make architectural decisions—understand when a fixed-size state is enough, when it becomes a bottleneck, and when you want to combine it with something else.
